Learning Objectives
Specify the components of a thorough patient history and physical examination to create a
differential diagnosis for elbow pathology.
Perform an appropriate physical examination of the elbow to guide a patient evaluation and
additional imaging studies, if indicated.
Specify individual components of the physical examination to improve clinical diagnosis.
Identify deficits that may guide physiotherapy and treatment options to avoid and manage
injuries.

Elbow pathology can be categorized as traumatic, degenerative, congenital, inflammatory, or
associated with systemic conditions (malignancy).
Elbow mechanics are substantially influenced by shoulder and wrist motion and function.
The proximity of regional peripheral nerve anatomy to the elbow capsule and osseous
anatomy may predispose patients to specific conditions.
Pediatric patients and the younger overhead athlete population (throwers, swimmers,
gymnasts) often have high levels of load applied across their elbows, predisposing them to
specific conditions.
Draping/Patient Positioning

Draping/Patient Positioning
Circumferential visual access to the cervical spine and shoulder and the elbows,
forearms, and hands bilaterally is necessary. In general, the physical examination is
performed with the patient in a sitting position. Some tests for lateral instability require
supine positioning of the patient with the arm above the head. A thorough elbow
examination requires evaluation of the cervical spine and the shoulder to assess for
radicular processes and shoulder motion restrictions/weakness/scapular dyskinesia.
General Inspection
The elbow is examined for incisions/scars, regions of swelling/erythema, muscle atrophy, and
asymmetry. Intra-articular elbow effusions may be appreciated by examining for loss of the
normal lateral dimple in the anconeus triangle.
In patients in whom the long head of the biceps tendon has ruptured, a Popeye deformity may
be present. In patients with a retracted distal biceps tendon rupture, a reverse Popeye
deformity may be present.

General Inspection

The presence of bony/soft-tissue deformities, including abnormalities of the carrying
angle of the elbow, is noted. Cubitus valgus of 11° to 14° in men and 13° to 16° in
women is normal (measured with full extension of the arm and supination of the
forearm). The elbows on both sides of the body are compared.
Limb Mechanical Evaluation
Scapular dyskinesia, rotator cuff pathology, and other conditions of the shoulder girdle may
have profound effects on elbow motion and function.
Evaluate shoulder motion and scapular rhythm by observing the patient from behind as
he/she brings the upper extremities into forward elevation. Examine shoulder motion and
assess for prominent impingement signs, posterior shoulder capsule tightness, and
glenohumeral internal rotation deficits.
Palpation
Laterally, the landmarks of the elbow include the lateral epicondyle, origin of the common
extensor tendon, posterior interosseous nerve, radiocapitellar joint, radial head, and
capitellum.
Medially, the examiner should assess the ulnotrochlear joint, medial epicondyle, cubital
tunnel/ulnar nerve, and origin of the common flexor tendon.
Posteriorly, the olecranon and bursa, proximal radioulnar joint, and triceps tendon can be
palpated.
Anteriorly, the sublime tubercle and the distal biceps tendon should be examined (Videos 1, 2,
3, and 4).


Palpation
The anatomic landmarks of the elbow are palpated for evidence of swelling, warmth,
tenderness, deformity, and instability. If a painful structure is encountered during
palpation, then the examiner should determine whether it reproduces the patient’s
typical symptoms.
Range of Motion Tests
Active range of motion (ROM) can be assessed with the patient in a sitting or standing position.
The following movements are observed: elbow flexion/extension and pronation/supination
with the elbow in 90° of flexion. Passive ROM is subsequently assessed, and limitations are
noted.
Both elbows are examined simultaneously, and differences in rhythm and maximum achieved
ROM are noted. Table 1 depicts normal values for flexion/extension and pronation/supination
of the elbow.1

The relationship between pain and ROM should be assessed. Mid-arc pain may indicate acute
joint inflammation, whereas end-arc pain is associated with joint contractures and
osteoarthritis (Videos 5 and 6).

Strength Tests

Strength Tests
The patient is examined in the sitting or standing position with the elbow flexed to 90°
and the forearm in neutral rotation. Each motion is isolated and assessed in sequence.
Strength is graded based on the Medical Research Council scale. Resisted elbow flexion
and extension are assessed. In general, extension power is 70% of flexion power.
Resisted pronation and supination also are assessed. In general, pronation power is 80%
of supination power. Provocation of pain with resisted movements should be noted
(Videos 7, 8, 9 and 10).

Provocative Tests/Special Tests
Instability
Varus/valgus—The patient is placed in a seated position with the shoulder fully externally
rotated to stabilize movement through the glenohumeral joint. The elbow is flexed to 30° to
disengage the olecranon from its fossa (which, in full extension, will lock the elbow and give a
false sense of stability). Gapping may be difficult to assess as described below; however, pain
and instability may be determined with these examination maneuvers.
The lateral ligament complex and the lateral ulnar collateral ligament, specifically, is
assessed with the application of a varus stress, with palpation for any gapping at the
radiocapitellar interval. The forearm should be supinated during this maneuver to relax the
lateral forearm extensors, which act as secondary stabilizers (Video 11).

To evaluate for instability on the medial side of the elbow, a valgus stress is applied, and
the examiner palpates for any gapping at the ulnotrochlear joint. If present, this may
indicate insufficiency of the medial collateral ligament. The forearm should be pronated
during this maneuver to relax the medial forearm flexors, which act as secondary
stabilizers (Figure 1; Video 12).

Moving valgus stress test—Described for athletes involved in throwing who have
symptomatic attenuation of the medial collateral ligament, this test involves abduction of the
shoulder to 90°. A valgus force is applied to the elbow, and the elbow is then brought quickly
through a complete arc from flexion to full extension. Pain experienced at 70° to 120° of this
arc may indicate symptomatic insufficiency of the medial collateral ligament2 (Figure 2).

Milking maneuver test—The patient positions the arm in adduction and external rotation at
the shoulder, with the elbow flexed more than 90°. The patient then reaches the
contralateral arm under the elbow in question and, with the hand of the contralateral arm,
applies traction to the thumb of the adducted and externally rotated arm, which creates a
valgus moment across the elbow. The reproduction of pain across the medial aspect of the
elbow constitutes a positive test result1 (Figure 3; Video 13).

Posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI): In patients with PLRI, the proximal radius and ulna
remain as a unit, with a normal congruent articulation at the proximal radioulnar joint.
Together, they rotate externally off the distal humerus in a spectrum of instability ranging
from posterolateral subluxation of the radial head to full posterior ulnotrochlear dislocation. In
general, insufficiency of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament and the radial collateral ligament is
required for PLRI. This differs from proximal radioulnar joint instability, which is observed in
patients with a Monteggia fracture.
PLRI (lateral pivot shift) test—The patient is placed in the supine position, and the affected
arm is brought overhead. The humerus is stabilized, and the elbow is extended. With the
elbow extended, the forearm is supinated, and a valgus, axially directed load is applied to the
elbow. In this position, the proximal ulna and radius are subluxated at the ulnotrochlear and
radiocapitellar joints, respectively. The elbow is then progressively flexed, and a sense of
apprehension accompanies the flexion. In patients with PLRI, the unit consisting of the
proximal ulna and the radial head will reduce beyond 40° of flexion (the position of maximal
displacement). Before this reduction occurs, a lateral skin dimple may be noted proximal to
the radial head. Reduction is manifested by a palpable clunk as the radial head reduces. This
test is a challenge to perform in patients who are awake because patients often have
difficulty relaxing sufficiently to allow for proper performance of the test1 (Figure 4).

Figure 4 Illustration shows the posterolateral rotatory instability test. (Reproduced from
Matache BA, Gammon B, Athwal GS, Bicknell RT: Physical examination of the shoulder and

Posterolateral drawer test—The elbow is flexed to 30°, and an anteroposterior force is
applied to subluxate the ulna and radius off the distal humerus. The test is repeated in 90° of
flexion, and a sensation of instability or palpable subluxation indicates a positive test result.
The posterolateral rotatory drawer test is similar to this test; however, in the posterolateral
drawer test, a hypersupination force is applied to the forearm, resulting in abnormal
excessive posterolateral subluxation of the elbow.
Push-up and chair-press tests—In the prone position, the patient attempts to push up from
the floor with the forearms maximally supinated and the hands spaced wider than the
shoulders. This applies a valgus, posteriorly directed load to the elbow. A positive test result
consists of apprehension or instability as the elbow progresses from flexion to extension.
The chair-press test is a variation in which the patient pushes up and out of a chair with the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:44 PM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Elbow
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000585
17/28

palms of the hands facing inward on the armrests, thus maximally supinating the forearm.
Similar to the push-up test, the valgus, posteriorly directed forces across the elbow will
aggravate symptoms of instability at approximately 40° of flexion. Relief of symptoms if the
test is repeated with the forearm pronated (palms out) indicates a positive test result.
Plicae: Mechanical snapping with movement of the elbow through ROM may be related to
intra-articular plicae. Plicae may cause inflammation and secondary chondromalacia over time.
The flexion-pronation test assesses for plicae in the anterolateral radiocapitellar joint. The
elbow is passively flexed in full pronation, and a painful snap is felt.
The extension-supination test assesses for posterolateral plicae affecting the radiocapitellar
joint. The elbow is passively extended in full supination, and a painful snap is felt.
Cubitus varus may alter the vector of pull for the triceps muscle, causing the distal triceps
tendon to subluxate over the medial epicondyle of the humerus. In symptomatic patients,
this is termed a snapping medial triceps. This condition also occurs in patients with
hypertrophied triceps muscles, such as weightlifters.
Distal biceps tendon: Ruptures of the distal biceps tendon often manifest as pain and
swelling in the antecubital fossa. Resisted flexion of the elbow and supination of the forearm
may be painful in patients with a partial tear. If the ruptured tendon is retracted, a reverse
Popeye deformity may be present. The biceps crease interval can be determined by fully
extending and supinating the elbow and measuring the distance between the main elbow
flexion crease in the antecubital fossa and the distalmost aspect of the biceps muscle in its
central axis. A biceps crease interval of more than 6 cm is predictive of a distal biceps tendon
rupture. Normally, the belly of the biceps muscle should rise and fall with active flexion and
extension of the elbow. The hook test can be used to evaluate for a rupture of the distal
biceps tendon. In this test, the patient flexes the elbow to 90° and fully supinates the
forearm. The examiner’s distal phalanx is inserted laterally beneath the distal biceps, hooking
it and pulling the tendon forward. Inability to perform the hook test indicates a distal biceps
tear1 (Figure 5).

Medial epicondylitis: Also termed golfer’s elbow, medial epicondylitis involves degeneration
and tendinosis of the common flexor origin at its attachment on the medial epicondyle.
Direct palpation of this area will reproduce pain. Pain also may be reproduced with resisted
flexion of the wrist and pronation of the forearm or with passive wrist and elbow extension
with supination. These tests stress the abnormal tissue and exacerbate symptoms, especially
if performed in combination with direct palpation of the insertion of the common flexor
tendon. Grip strength on the patient’s affected side should be compared with that on the
opposite side.
Lateral epicondylitis: Also termed tennis elbow, lateral epicondylitis involves degeneration
and tendinosis of the tendon of the extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle at its origin on the
lateral epicondyle of the humerus. Direct palpation of this area will reproduce pain. Pain also
may be reproduced with resisted wrist and long finger extension with the elbow in full
extension (Maudsley test) or with passive wrist and elbow flexion with pronation. These

Long finger test, in Sarwark JF, ed: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 4. Rosemont, IL,

Ulnar nerve: Although it is important to examine all the nerves about the elbow in patients
with elbow disorders, the ulnar nerve may be especially affected. Therefore, the ulnar nerve
should be evaluated closely for comorbid neuritis, subluxation, and compression.
In examining the ulnar nerve, the examiner should palpate its course through a flexion-
extension arc, assessing for evidence of subluxation over the medial epicondyle (which is
particularly important if elbow arthroscopy is being considered because the procedure is
relatively contraindicated in patients with ulnar nerve instability).
The Tinel sign is identified by percussing the ulnar nerve along its length for signs of
irritability. To exacerbate compression symptoms, the elbow is held in hyperflexion with
the wrist extended for 1 minute, which is a procedure analogous to the Phalen test at the
wrist. Reproduction of numbness or paresthesia in the ulnar two digits of the hand is
noted. The most common site of compression is at the cubital tunnel.

(flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint with pinching).

Neurologic Examination
Elbow function may be affected by neurologic and muscular conditions ranging from cerebral
to cervical spine to peripheral nerve conditions, such as a stroke, Parkinson disease, cervical
stenosis and radiculitis, peripheral nerve entrapment syndromes, and amyotrophic lateral
sclerosis.
Sensory Examination
The sensory examination focuses on the C5-T1 dermatomes in the distributions of the axillary,
musculocutaneous, radial, median, and ulnar nerves.
Special attention to the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve during distal biceps repair, the
medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve during medial approaches (eg, medial ulnar collateral
ligament reconstruction)
Special attention to peripheral nerve entrapment examinations for radial tunnel (radial),
cubital tunnel (ulnar), and pronator syndrome (median)
Digital two-point discrimination in the median and ulnar nerve distributions may be helpful
for additional sensitivity and details.
Motor Examination
The motor examination is an extension of the sensory examination to assess the axillary,
musculocutaneous, radial, median, and ulnar nerves.
Reflexes
The biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis reflexes are elicited with the use of a reflex hammer.

Other Tests
Electromyography/nerve conduction studies

Other Tests
Electromyography/nerve conduction studies may be helpful in evaluating brachial
plexopathy, cubital tunnel and ulnar neuropathy, pronator syndrome, carpal tunnel and
median neuropathy, and other neuromuscular conditions about the elbow.
Imaging Studies
Radiography

Radiography
Plain radiographs, including orthogonal views, are essential to visualize the osseous
anatomy of the elbow. Radiocapitellar oblique views may aid in identifying fractures and
osteochondritis dissecans. Hyperflexion lateral views may help identify posterior
compartment osteophytes and loose bodies in patients with valgus extension overload
and medial ulnar collateral ligament insufficiency3 (Figure 6).

CT scans may be helpful in patients with trauma and may aid in identifying
osteochondritis dissecans and occult loose bodies. Three-dimensional CT reconstruction
may help in planning more complex arthroplasty procedures, osteotomies, and
reconstruction procedures.

bodies, collateral ligament compromise, pigmented villonodular synovitis, extensor carpi
radialis brevis and associated lateral epicondyle pathology, and other conditions4 (Figure 7).
